strengths: Addresses a timely and practically relevant problem—high-resolution (1K/2K) instruction-based image editing—which is under-explored relative to low-resolution editing.

The core idea is clean and well-motivated: delegate semantic editing to an existing low-resolution editor and transfer fine-grained source details into the high-resolution target via a learnable feature-space transfer function (a 1×1 conv on intermediate features) optimized at test time.

The patch synchronization mechanism (blended Tweedie updates + resampling) is technically interesting and, per the ablations (Figs. 5, 7), demonstrably reduces boundary artifacts while avoiding overlapping inference, reducing compute relative to prior tiled approaches.
Reasonable breadth of components: transfer function design with spatial adaptivity (vs. a global constant vector), a τ hyperparameter for detail/content trade-off, and an ablation over τ (Table 2).
Generalization is demonstrated across two backbones (Stable Diffusion v2.1 and the transformer-based FLUX.1-dev), which strengthens the robustness claim.
Clear organization, pseudo-code in the appendix, and use of publicly available models support a reasonable degree of reproducibility.
Quantitative results (Table 1) show consistent, if modest, improvements over SR-based baselines on the reported masked metrics.
weaknesses: Evaluation metrics are exclusively low-level reconstruction/fidelity measures (M-MSE, M-SSIM, M-PSNR, HaarPSI). For an editing task, there is no semantic/text-alignment metric (e.g., CLIP or instruction-following accuracy) and no human study, so it is not directly demonstrated that the edits actually follow the instruction correctly—only that source details are preserved.

The baselines are super-resolution methods (DiT-SR, DiT4SR, PiSA-SR, TSD-SR) applied to low-resolution edits. These are not designed for the editing task, making the comparison somewhat of a straw man. Stronger, more directly comparable baselines (e.g., MultiDiffusion/DemoFusion-style tiled diffusion editing, or other high-resolution editing pipelines) are not evaluated.

No computational cost analysis (runtime, memory, number of test-time optimization steps) is reported, despite test-time optimization plus patch-wise processing being the central mechanism. This is a material omission for a method whose practicality hinges on overhead.

The framing as a 'high-resolution editing' contribution is partially overstated: the actual semantic edit is performed by an external low-resolution model (NanoBanana/Gemini), and the method largely performs reference-conditioned detail transfer/super-resolution. Consequently, output quality is upper-bounded by the low-resolution reference, as the authors acknowledge in the Limitations.

The 'first to propose high-resolution image editing' claim is not adequately substantiated against prior high-resolution synthesis/editing work (e.g., tiled-diffusion and high-resolution diffusion synthesis lines of work).
The masked metrics depend on LANG-SAM-generated masks, so results are partially confounded by mask quality, which is not ablated.
Gains on some metrics are marginal (e.g., 2K HaarPSI 0.331 vs. 0.316; M-PSNR 21.955 vs. 21.379), and no significance or variance analysis is provided.
The evaluation set (400 image/instruction pairs) is synthesized via FreeScale with ChatGPT-generated prompts and instructions, which may not reflect real-world editing distributions.

strengths: Introduces and formalizes high-resolution image editing as a task, addressing a practical need for controllable high-resolution content creation beyond 1K resolution.
Proposes ScaleEdit, a test-time optimization framework that reuses pretrained low-resolution editing priors instead of retraining diffusion models for high resolution.

Develops a detail enhancement module using a learnable transfer function on intermediate diffusion features, optimized by aligning low-resolution reverse trajectories with high-resolution source trajectories; it is lightweight (1x1 conv) and applicable to both U-Net (Stable Diffusion) and transformer (FLUX) backbones.

Introduces a patch synchronization strategy with blended Tweedie updates and resampling that reduces boundary artifacts without overlapping inference, lowering computational overhead relative to overlapping patch schemes.

Provides quantitative and qualitative evidence: outperforms SR-based baselines on 1K and 2K editing across MSE, SSIM, PSNR, HaarPSI, and masked variants; includes ablations on synchronization and τ, and demonstrates generality to FLUX.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter inconsistency: the main text states τ=15, while Appendix Table 2 states that the default τ=35 achieves the best performance across all metrics. It is unclear which setting produced the main results, which undermines reproducibility and the claimed optimal configuration.

Evaluation is limited to a single low-resolution editor (NanoBanana) combined with SR baselines; no comparison to direct high-resolution editing methods (e.g., multi-diffusion or tiling-based editing) or other high-resolution generation/editing approaches, so the state-of-the-art claim is not fully established.

The method depends on the quality of an external low-resolution reference editor; artifacts or semantic errors from that editor propagate to the high-resolution output. The limitations section acknowledges this but no mitigation or robustness analysis is provided.

The feature transfer function is optimized on the low-resolution source trajectory and then applied to the target trajectory; there is no quantitative analysis of how well this transfers across different editing types (object replacement, style transfer, background modification) or how sensitive it is to source-target semantic gaps.

The synchronization ablation is qualitative only (Figures 5 and 7); there are no quantitative boundary-artifact metrics or runtime/FLOPs comparisons to substantiate the claimed computational benefit of avoiding overlapping inference.

The claim of being 'the first' to propose high-resolution image editing may be overclaimed, and related work does not sufficiently discuss prior high-resolution synthesis/editing approaches based on tiling or multi-diffusion. The description of timestep τ is also confusing relative to the diffusion reverse process.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: high-resolution image editing beyond the native operating resolution of diffusion models, where users increasingly need to modify existing high-res assets rather than synthesize new ones.

The patch-wise strategy that matches the diffusion model's native receptive field is well motivated, and Appendix E gives a reasonable argument for why tiling preserves micro-scale detail better than architectural modifications (e.g., FreeScale).

The blended-Tweedie synchronization mechanism is technically creative: it uses an auxiliary blended latent to harmonize denoising trajectories at patch boundaries without overlapping-view sampling, and the ablation in Figures 5 and 7 provides some visual evidence that it reduces boundary artifacts.
The framework is shown to generalize to a transformer backbone (FLUX.1-dev) in addition to Stable Diffusion, suggesting the approach is not tied to a specific architecture.
The manuscript is generally clearly written, with a readable overview figure, pseudo-code in the appendix, and ablations over the hyperparameter τ and the synchronization module.
weaknesses: The evaluation is fundamentally unfair to the baselines and therefore does not support the central claim of superiority. The SR baselines operate on the low-resolution edited image with no access to the high-resolution source, whereas ScaleEdit conditions on the high-resolution source. The comparison thus largely confirms the obvious (that using the high-res source helps) rather than isolating the method's contribution.

The proposed metrics are biased toward the method: M-MSE/M-SSIM/M-PSNR are computed in 'should-be-unchanged' regions using masks derived from LANG-SAM, i.e., they measure source preservation. Since only ScaleEdit has access to the high-res source, it wins these metrics almost by construction. Critically, none of the metrics measure whether the edit itself succeeded semantically (no CLIP/DINO alignment, instruction-following accuracy, or user study), which is a material gap for an editing paper claiming 'state-of-the-art editing capacity.'

The most relevant prior art is not compared against. The paper cites patch-/tiling-based high-resolution diffusion methods (MultiDiffusion, DemoFusion, ScaleCrafter, FreeScale, Diffusion4K) but never benchmarks against them; these are the natural strong baselines for the high-resolution setting and their absence weakens the empirical case.

Reproducibility is a significant concern. The pipeline depends on NanoBanana (proprietary Gemini 2.5 Flash Image API) to produce the low-res reference and on ChatGPT for instructions, and no code or dataset release is mentioned. Results therefore cannot be independently reproduced or fairly compared.

There is an internal inconsistency regarding hyperparameters: Section 5.1 states τ = 15 is used in the main experiments, while Appendix D claims τ = 35 is the 'default setting' and best. This undermines confidence in the reported configuration and the τ ablation.

The 'resampling strategy' is an approximation introduced to avoid computing Δh for auxiliary latents; its justification is heuristic and not rigorously validated, and it is unclear how much it degrades synchronization quality relative to the exact formulation.

Novelty is moderate. Patch-wise high-res diffusion and feature injection through test-time optimization are established ideas; the contribution is mainly their combination with the blended-Tweedie synchronization. The claim of being 'the first to propose the high-resolution image editing task' is strong and arguably overstated given prior high-resolution i2i/generation work.

The quantitative gains in Table 1 are modest (e.g., HaarPSI 0.342 vs. 0.335; M-SSIM 0.739 vs. 0.695) and reported without significance testing. The paper also claims synchronization 'meaningfully reduces computational overhead' but provides no runtime or memory comparisons to substantiate this.

The transfer function is under-specified: it is unclear whether θ is shared across timesteps or optimized per-timestep, how many parameters are trained, or how the detail-transfer behavior evolves over the reverse process. These details matter for assessing cost and generality.

Qualitative comparisons in Figure 4 are inconclusive in several rows (e.g., the sunset-sky and green-valley examples) where baselines appear comparable, and the reliance on cherry-picked zoom-ins without quantitative semantic evaluation weakens the evidence.

strengths: Introduces and formalizes a practically relevant task: high-resolution image editing beyond 1K, with explicit problem formulation and evaluation settings for 1K/2K editing.
Proposes a test-time optimization framework that leverages pretrained diffusion/flow models without training a new generative model from scratch.

The patch-wise detail transfer module using a lightweight learnable 1x1 convolution on intermediate features is simple and compatible with both U-Net (Stable Diffusion) and transformer/flow backbones (FLUX).
The synchronization strategy based on blended Tweedie estimates and resampling avoids overlapping inference, which can reduce computational overhead compared with overlapping-patch approaches.

Provides quantitative comparisons on 1K/2K editing, qualitative results, ablations on the transfer function, synchronization, and hyperparameter tau, plus pseudo-code and implementation details in the supplementary material.
Demonstrates generalization beyond Stable Diffusion to FLUX and shows qualitative 8K editing results, supporting the claim that the framework is not tied to one backbone.
weaknesses: The main quantitative evaluation mostly measures source-preservation/reconstruction quality (M-MSE, M-SSIM, M-PSNR, LPIPS, HaarPSI) rather than instruction-following or semantic editing correctness. A CLIP-based instruction-alignment metric is only used in a small ablation on transfer-function design, not in the main 1K/2K comparisons, so the central editing claim is not quantitatively well supported.

Baselines are limited to low-resolution editing followed by super-resolution (DiT-SR, DiT4SR, PiSA-SR, TSD-SR). There is no comparison against dedicated high-resolution generation/editing approaches such as tiled-diffusion, MultiDiffusion-style methods, HD-Painter, or other high-resolution editing/generation frameworks, making the 'state-of-the-art' claim weaker than stated.

The claim that the method 'consistently outperforms all baselines' is contradicted by Table 1: in 2K editing, PiSA-SR achieves better LPIPS (0.472) than ScaleEdit (0.496). This factual overstatement should be corrected and discussed.

Reproducibility is a significant concern: the low-resolution edited references are produced by the proprietary Nana Banana/Gemini 2.5 model, prompts are generated with ChatGPT, and no code release or reproducible benchmark is mentioned. This makes the exact experimental pipeline difficult to reproduce or fairly compare against.

Computational cost is high and not fully characterized: for 1K editing, the method requires 20.29 GB VRAM, 234.77 seconds without Null-text inversion and 635.51 seconds with it, while no runtime/memory results are reported for 2K or 8K. This weakens the scalability claim and raises practical-usability concerns.

The method relies on a low-resolution edited reference image; artifacts introduced by the low-resolution editor can propagate to the high-resolution output, as acknowledged in the limitations. This dependency is central to the framework but is not quantitatively analyzed.

Evaluation is relatively small-scale: 100 synthetic source images / 400 pairs for the main quantitative study, plus 285 real images in the appendix. The ablation studies use only 60 pairs, and no statistical significance or human evaluation is provided.

The related-work discussion does not adequately cover prior high-resolution editing/inpainting methods; it primarily contrasts with low-resolution editing and diffusion-based super-resolution. This weakens the novelty positioning and may miss important baselines.

Some technical details of the synchronization mechanism are underspecified in the main text, especially handling of corner patches and multi-neighbor blending, which could affect reproducibility and boundary consistency.

strengths: Introduces and formalizes a genuinely useful and under-explored task—high-resolution (2K/4K/8K) instruction-based image editing—with a clean formulation that leverages low-resolution reference edits as semantic guides while preserving high-resolution source detail. The motivation (existing editors cap at ~1K; naive edit+SR loses micro-texture because SR is source-unconditional) is well argued.

The core technical idea is principled and non-obvious: rather than a single global constant feature offset, the transfer function is defined as a feature-adaptive operator (a 1x1 conv on intermediate features of the frozen generator), which the ablation in Table 3 and the cat-to-dog discussion justify as necessary for spatially varying edits.

The synchronization strategy is a real methodological contribution: the blended-Tweedie formulation with linearly ramped interpolation weights, combined with a resampling step that avoids redefining Delta-h for auxiliary latents (Eq. 13), achieves patch consistency without overlapping inference, avoiding the compute penalty of MultiDiffusion-style approaches. Ablations (Fig. 5a, Fig. 9, Table 2/3) support this.

Experimental evidence is broad for a new task: quantitative comparison against four strong SR baselines on both 1K and 2K editing (Table 1) with five metrics including source-aware masked variants (M-MSE/M-SSIM/M-PSNR via LANG-SAM), plus qualitative comparisons, real-image results (Fig. 7, Table 4), 8K scaling (Fig. 6), and generalization to the transformer-based FLUX backbone (Fig. 5b), which demonstrates the framework is not U-Net-specific.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: implementation details (Stable Diffusion v2.1-base, T=50, tau=15), adaptation details for both U-Net and FLUX (Sec. C), pseudo-code (Alg. 1), and explicit equations for blending masks and the vector-field modification (Eqs. 15-27).
Honest discussion of limitations, computational cost (Sec. G), and societal impact; the paper does not over-claim and correctly scopes itself to a low-res-reference-driven editing paradigm.
weaknesses: The baseline family is narrow: all quantitative baselines are low-res-edit + SR pipelines (DiT-SR, DiT4SR, PiSA-SR, TSD-SR). Given the paper's central claim that patch-wise denoising without synchronization causes seams, the natural alternative—overlapping-patch high-resolution generation/editing such as MultiDiffusion or SyncDiffusion—is neither compared against quantitatively nor qualitatively, nor is a 'patch-wise framework without the transfer function' ablation reported. This weakens the evidence that the proposed transfer function (not merely the patch scheme) is what enables detail transfer.

Main quantitative evaluation uses 100 synthetically generated (FreeScale) 4K images downsampled to 2K/1K, with references produced by a single editor (Nano Banana) and instructions from ChatGPT; this makes results sensitive to the reference editor's quality and leaves real-image evaluation (285 pairs) only in the supplement. A larger, more diverse, and ideally real-image benchmark with human or VLM preference judgments would better validate editing fidelity vs. mere source preservation.

LPIPS and HaarPSI are computed against the source image, which rewards retention of source pixels rather than successful editing; combined with the masked metrics, the evaluation may under-credit edits that legitimately alter regions. The paper acknowledges LPIPS is a weak proxy but does not add a direct editing-accuracy measure (e.g., CLIP-Sim is only used in the supplementary ablation).

Runtime is a significant practical concern: 234.77 s per image without NTI and 635.51 s with NTI at 20.29 GB VRAM in full precision, versus 0.74-88 s for baselines. Since the method is test-time optimization applied per image and per edit, the paper's claim of efficiency relative to overlapping-inference synchronization is somewhat offset by an overall cost that may limit real deployment; no attempt is made to quantify the amortized benefit of the resampling strategy versus an overlap-based baseline.

The claim of being 'the first' to propose high-resolution image editing is strong given prior work on high-resolution synthesis/editing (e.g., ScaleCrafter and related scale-based editing); a clearer positioning against these would avoid over-claiming.

The patch-wise design may break globally coherent structure for edits spanning multiple patches or involving long-range consistency; the paper does not analyze failure modes beyond boundary seams (e.g., a large object being split or edited inconsistently across patches), which is a natural concern for the proposed paradigm.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant task (high-resolution image editing, beyond 1K) with clear real-world motivation, and frames the problem setting (high-res source + low-res reference) reasonably clearly.

The patch-wise inference design that matches the generative model's native resolution, together with a non-overlapping synchronization mechanism, is a sensible engineering solution that avoids the cost of overlapping-window sampling.

Demonstrates generalization across two very different backbones (Stable Diffusion v2.1 and FLUX.1-dev) and shows qualitative scalability up to 8K, suggesting the framework is not tied to one architecture.

Includes ablation studies on the transfer-function design, the hyperparameter tau, and the synchronization strategy, with a supplementary pseudo-code and implementation details that aid reproducibility of the proposed components.
The synchronization strategy (blended Tweedie estimate + resampling) is a nontrivial technical contribution that plausibly reduces boundary artifacts without overlapping inference.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core recipe (edit at low resolution, then transfer fine-grained detail back to high resolution) is largely intuitive, and the central 'learnable transfer function' is just a per-timestep 1x1 convolution applied to intermediate features, which is a very lightweight and incremental module.

Questionable baselines and an evaluation strawman: the only comparison is against super-resolution methods (DiT-SR, DiT4SR, PiSA-SR, TSD-SR) bolted onto a low-resolution editor. No comparison is made against methods that can natively operate at the target resolution or against recent high-resolution generation/editing approaches (e.g., FreeScale, ScaleCrafter, SDXL-based or KV-Edit/Step1X-Edit style editors adapted to higher resolutions), so the 'state-of-the-art' claim is not well supported.

Marginal quantitative gains: in Table 1 the improvements are small (e.g., HaarPSI 0.342 vs. 0.335, M-MSE 0.054 vs. 0.058), and on 2K LPIPS the proposed method (0.496) is actually worse than PiSA-SR (0.472). This does not convincingly establish a substantial advantage.

Heavy dependence on an external low-resolution editor (Nano Banana) to produce the reference image: the method is essentially a detail-transfer module layered on top of an existing low-res editing pipeline, and the paper itself notes in the Limitations that artifacts from the low-res reference propagate to the final output. This undercuts the framing of a complete high-resolution editing solution.
The claim of being 'the first to propose the high-resolution image editing task' is overstated and insufficiently justified against prior work on high-resolution image generation and manipulation.

Computational cost is high and inadequately addressed: 20.29 GB VRAM and 234.77 seconds runtime are reported, with only a speculative statement that future refinement will bring efficiency gains. No concrete efficiency improvement is demonstrated.

Evaluation breadth is limited: roughly 100 source images and 400 (image, instruction) pairs, with ablations on only 60 pairs; no user study is conducted, and the 8K scenario (Figure 6) has no quantitative evaluation at all.

The synchronization section is very complex (blended Tweedie estimates with multiple masks, translation operators, and interpolation weights), but its benefit is demonstrated only qualitatively (Figure 5a, Figure 9), with no quantitative ablation of the synchronization components in the main results.

Reproducibility is weakened by reliance on a proprietary/unavailable low-resolution editor and by the intricacy of the synchronization and resampling procedure, which is only partially specified in the main text.
